headline: The pope's message to Milei: people before the economy.
summary: Pope Leo XIV arrived in Buenos Aires on Sunday, the first papal visit to Argentina in nearly 40 years. In his first speech he told President Javier Milei's officials that 'the economy must serve the person, not the person the economy'. Milei's spending cuts took inflation from 200% to about 32%, and roughly 300,000 formal jobs vanished.

cover_question.q: Is the pope the boss of a president?

cover_answer: No. He can only say his piece. He said it, with Milei there.
table_question: Should a guest say what they think of how you run your house?

5-7.script: The pope flew to Argentina on Sunday, the first pope to visit in almost 40 years, and people waited in a square with banners to see him. He told the country's leaders to look after people first and money second. Like a coach who says the team matters more than the score. Nobody is in trouble. It was a visit.
5-7.why: The crowd with banners is the story at six. The economics stay off the card.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them the crowd with banners and a coach who puts the team before the score, and keeps inflation and pensions off the card. Expect 'does the pope live there now?' No. He is on a 12-day trip to three countries, and then he goes home.

8-12.script: Argentina's president, Javier Milei, cut government spending hard. Inflation fell from 200% to about 32%, but around 300,000 jobs disappeared. On Sunday the pope arrived and said the economy must serve people, not the other way round. Like a referee reminding both teams what the game is for.
8-12.why: A chain with a real trade-off in it, which is what they weigh at ten.
8-12.why_long: Between eight and twelve a child is working out cause and effect, so the script hands them a real trade-off: cuts that tamed inflation and cost 300,000 jobs, and a visitor who says people come first. The referee is the mechanism. Expect 'so who's right?' Say both facts are true and ask which one they would weigh more.

13-17.script: Can a guest criticise his host without naming him? Pope Leo told Argentina's leaders Sunday 'the economy must serve the person, not the person the economy', with Milei, who calls social justice 'theft', welcoming him. Second: his cuts took inflation from 200% to 32% and 300,000 jobs went. Success?
13-17.why: Guest and host, cuts and jobs: two pairs they can hold at fifteen.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once, so the script hands them two pairs: a guest who rebukes his host without saying his name, and cuts that cut inflation and cut jobs. Expect 'isn't the pope supposed to stay out of politics?' Say he quoted 60 years of church teaching on it, and let them decide where the line is.

5-7.q: Is the pope the boss of a president?
5-7.a: No. He leads the Catholic Church, not Argentina. He can say what he thinks, and the leaders decide what to do with it.

8-12.q: Why does the pope care about money?
8-12.a: Church teaching has said so for 60 years. Leo quoted earlier popes.
No. He welcomed him and said some occasions 'transcend our differences'.

13-17.a: He never named him. He quoted decades of church teaching instead.

13-17.q: Why the first papal visit in 40 years?
13-17.a: Pope Francis was Argentine and never went home in his 12 years as pope. The article doesn't say why.
